question: A wire of length L and resistance R is reformed so that its length increases by 50% with no change in its volume. The resistance of the new wire is:
solution:
The correct answer is **__((9)/(4)) R__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.**
 
• We can use the formula: 
 
 
• ​R = ρL/A
 
 
 
• where: 
 
 
• R is the resistance
 
• ρ is the resistivity of the material
 
• L is the length of the wire
 
• A is the cross-sectional area of the wire
 
 
 
• Therefore, the new resistance is:
 
 
• R' = ρ(1.5L) / (2/3A) = (9/4)ρL/A = (9/4)R
 
 
 
• If the length of the wire increases by 50%, the new length becomes 1.5L.
 
• **Since the volume of the wire remains constant, the cross-sectional area must decrease by a factor of 2/3 to maintain the same volume.**** **
 
• Therefore, the new resistance is:
 
 
• R' = ρ(1.5L) / (2/3A) = (9/4)ρL/A = (9/4)R
 
 
 
• So, the resistance of the new wire is **(9/4) times** the resistance of the original wire.
